verdict.rationale: Converging verbs of real becoming and shared substance state that Jesus possesses a full human nature across several New Testament writings. John 1:14 uses 'become' (ginomai) in the aorist (a completed past action), in the clause 'the Word became flesh' (ho logos sarx egeneto), a verb of entering a state of being, not a verb of seeming. Hebrews 2:14 stacks 'shared in' (koinoneo) in the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) and 'partook of' (metecho) in the aorist (a completed past action), both governing 'blood and flesh' (haima kai sarx). Hebrews 2:16 sets angelic nature against 'the seed of Abraham' (sperma Abraam), Hebrews 2:17 and Hebrews 4:15 twice say 'according to all things' (kata panta), that is, like the brothers in every respect, and 1 John 4:2 makes the confession 'Jesus Christ having come in the flesh' (Iesoun Christon en sarki eleluthota), with the verb in the perfect participle (a settled, abiding state), a confessional test. Direct concordance work confirms the same 'become' (ginomai) plus 'flesh' (sarx) plus 'seed' (sperma) cluster in Romans 1:3, Philippians 2:7, and Galatians 4:4, so the pattern is broad, not isolated. Confidence is high because the witness is dense, comes from multiple authors, and the only readings that resist it are closed off by the becoming verbs and the predicated death. The verdict is not pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) because the words that carry the predication are New Testament-only, though Old Testament seed and resurrection texts are cross-referenced.

scripture.reasoning: The clause 'and the Word became flesh' (kai ho logos sarx egeneto) puts the aorist (a completed past action) 'became' (egeneto, from the dictionary form ginomai, confirmed in the store) together with 'flesh' (sarx) as the predicate. 'Become' (ginomai) is a verb of coming to be in a state, not a verb of appearing to be, so the Word came to exist as human flesh. 'He tabernacled among us' (eskenosen en hemin), that is, pitched his tent and lived with us, then locates that flesh dwelling among the community who saw glory, which fixes the becoming as concrete, not notional.

Two near-synonymous sharing verbs intensify the claim. 'The children have shared in' (ta paidia kekoinoneken, perfect tense of koinoneo, a completed action whose result still stands) 'blood and flesh' (haima kai sarx), and 'he himself in very like manner partook of' (autos paraplesios meteschen, aorist of metecho, a completed past action) 'the same things' (ton auton). 'In closely like manner' (paraplesios) means in nearly identical way, and the shared referent is human flesh and blood. The purpose clause 'so that through death' (hina dia tou thanatou) presupposes a mortal nature he can die in.

'He might release these, all who through fear of death throughout all life were held in slavery' (apallaxe toutous, hosoi phobo thanatou dia pantos tou zen enochoi esan douleias). The Son shares flesh and blood so that through his own death he frees those bound by fear of death. Death-capacity is stated about him, and the capacity to die is a feature of human nature, not of the divine nature, so the verse reinforces real humanity.

'For surely he does not take hold of angels but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham' (ou gar depou angelon epilambanetai alla spermatos Abraam epilambanetai). The 'not . . . but' (ou . . . alla) construction explicitly denies angelic nature and affirms 'the seed of Abraham' (sperma Abraam), that is human descent, as what is taken hold of. Even on the softer 'help' sense of 'take hold of' (epilambanomai), the recipients are still human seed, so the human reference is fixed either way.

'He was obligated to be made like the brothers according to all things' (opheilen kata panta tois adelphois homoiothenai). 'To be made like' (homoiothenai, from the dictionary form homoioo, confirmed in the store) is an aorist passive infinitive (a completed past action in the passive voice), and 'according to all things' (kata panta) is a universal quantifier, meaning in every respect. The obligation is tied to his function as a merciful and faithful 'high priest' (archiereus). The 'all' leaves no constituent of human nature reserved.

'Having been tested in every way according to the likeness, apart from sin' (pepeirasmenon kata panta kath' homoioteta choris hamartias). 'Having been tested' (pepeirasmenon, from the dictionary form peirazo) is a perfect passive participle (a settled state of having been tested). He was tested in every way according to the likeness of our condition, with 'sin' (hamartia) alone excluded. Genuine testing and 'sympathy' (sympatheo) presuppose a human will and emotional life that can actually be tested.

'Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in flesh is from God' (pan pneuma ho homologei Iesoun Christon en sarki eleluthota ek tou theou estin). 'Having come' (eleluthota, from the dictionary form erchomai, confirmed in the store) is a perfect active participle (a completed action whose result still stands), so the having come in flesh is a fixed, abiding state. 'In flesh' (en sarki) marks the embodied human nature as the very mode of the coming, which is the apostolic test of true confession.

'Every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God, and this is the spirit of the antichrist' (pan pneuma ho me homologei ton Iesoun ek tou theou ouk estin, kai touto estin to tou antichristou). The refusal to confess Jesus come in flesh is branded the spirit of 'antichrist' (antichristos). This flipside polemic presupposes that in-flesh coming is a non-negotiable confession, which confirms the positive statement of 1 John 4:2.

'The one who came to be from the seed of David according to flesh' (tou genomenou ek spermatos David kata sarka). Direct concordance shows the same word cluster as the anchors, 'become' (ginomai) plus 'seed' (sperma) plus 'flesh' (sarx), here stated about the Son. He came to be from the seed of David according to flesh, which is a literal human-descent statement and widens the pattern into the Pauline writings.

'In the likeness of men having come to be . . . and in form found as a man' (en homoiomati anthropon genomenos, lemma ginomai, confirmed in the store, kai schemati heuretheis hos anthropos). The participle of 'become' (ginomai) again says he came to be, and 'of men' (anthropon) names the kind. 'Likeness' (homoioma) carries a likeness sense that, taken alone, a reader could press toward appearance only, so this verse is both a witness and the place in the words where the contrary reading tries to enter.

'God sent forth his Son, having come to be from a woman, having come to be under law' (exapesteilen ho theos ton huion autou, genomenon ek gynaikos, genomenon hypo nomon). The store confirms 'having come to be' (genomenon, from the dictionary form ginomai) twice. 'Born of a woman' is a literal human-birth statement, the same 'become' verb (ginomai) used in John 1:14 and Romans 1:3, which extends the convergent pattern and roots it in ordinary human generation.

'In the likeness of sinful flesh' (en homoiomati sarkos hamartias). The store confirms 'likeness' (homoioma) plus 'flesh' (sarx) here. The phrase 'likeness of sinful flesh' is the strongest lexical foothold for a reading that softens the humanity, because 'likeness' (homoioma) can mean a copy or semblance. It is recorded as a complicating text, but the surrounding becoming and death verbs and the parallel plain statements in Romans 1:3 and Hebrews 2:14 prevent 'likeness' (homoioma) from meaning mere appearance.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'In the likeness of sinful flesh' (en homoiomati sarkos hamartias) uses 'likeness' (homoioma), which means likeness or semblance and in isolation could be pressed toward an appearance-only humanity. The store shows 'likeness' (homoioma) is rare, with only 6 occurrences, so its sense is set by context. Here the qualifier is 'of sin' (hamartias), not 'of flesh' (sarkos). The likeness is to SINFUL flesh, marking the absence of sin, not the absence of real flesh. The plain becoming statements Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 by the same author, and Hebrews 2:14 on sharing of flesh and blood, fix 'flesh' (sarx) as literal, so 'likeness' (homoioma) cannot reduce to mere appearance.

'In the likeness of men' (en homoiomati anthropon) and 'in form as a man' (schemati hos anthropos) pair 'likeness' (homoioma) with 'form or fashion' (schema), a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, or here near so) with a single store occurrence. Read alone these could suggest semblance. But the controlling verb is 'having come to be' (genomenos), the same 'become' verb (ginomai) of John 1:14, and the likeness language describes the real human condition he entered, not a costume. The verse stands as a witness to humanity once 'become' (ginomai) anchors it.

'Apart from sin' (choris hamartias) could be read as subtracting an integral part of the 'according to all things' (kata panta) likeness. The text distinguishes being tested from sinning. Sin is a defect in the exercise of human nature, not a constituent of it, so its absence preserves a non-fallen instance of full humanity rather than an incomplete one.

'Take hold of' (epilambanomai), with 19 occurrences, can mean take hold of a nature or help. On either sense the 'not . . . but' (ou . . . alla) contrast still locates the object in 'seed of Abraham' (spermatos Abraam), human descent, and Hebrews 2:14 and 2:17 settle assumed human nature on independent lexical grounds, so the verdict does not hang on resolving this verb.

variant_units_examined.note: The 'looses Jesus' (luei ton Iesoun) reading attested in some witnesses and church-father citation, versus the 'does not confess' (me homologei) reading present in the queried store text, does not change the verdict. Both readings target denial of Jesus come in flesh, so both presuppose the in-flesh confession as the apostolic norm.

variants.note: None of the anchor verses falls in the ingested ECM apparatus window (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) of 3 John 1:1 to 1:15, so no published apparatus was examined. The 1 John 4:3 location is handled from the queried store text and standard variant knowledge, and it is not verdict-flipping.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes 'become' (ginomai) in John 1:14, Romans 1:3, Philippians 2:7, Galatians 4:4 as a real change of state into the human condition, 'flesh' (sarx) and 'blood' (haima) as literal substance, and the predicated 'death' (thanatos) as genuine mortality. On this reading the 'according to all things' (kata panta) of Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15 closes off any reserved part of human nature, and 1 John 4:2 makes the confession a test.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: not sustainable on the lexical data
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: In its strongest form this lens leans on the likeness words, 'likeness' (homoioma) in Romans 8:3 and Philippians 2:7 and 'form' (schema) in Philippians 2:7, to argue that Jesus only seemed human. The lens is represented fairly because those words do carry a semblance sense. But 'become' (ginomai) is a becoming verb not a seeming verb, the flesh and blood are said to be shared and partaken, and his death is stated as the means of redemption, so the likeness words are qualified by real-becoming and real-dying language and cannot bear an appearance-only weight.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: not sustainable on the lexical data
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: In its strongest form this lens grants real flesh but reserves a higher human faculty, for example a rational soul, from the assumption. It is represented fairly because the bundle names 'flesh' (sarx) and 'blood' (haima) directly but does not carry a 'soul' (psyche) or 'mind' (nous) anchor word. The reading still fails because 'according to all things' (kata panta) in Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15 is an unrestricted universal, made like the brothers in every respect, and genuine 'testing' (peirazo) and 'sympathy' (sympatheo) require an interior human life, so no constituent is left reserved except sin.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on converging lexical evidence: 'become' (ginomai) plus 'flesh' (sarx) in John 1:14 and Romans 1:3, 'partook' (metecho) and 'shared' (koinoneo) plus 'flesh and blood' (sarx kai haima) in Hebrews 2:14, 'become' (ginomai) plus 'woman' (gyne) in Galatians 4:4, 'take hold of' (epilambanomai) plus 'seed of Abraham' (sperma Abraam) in Hebrews 2:16, 'make like' (homoioo) plus 'according to all things' (kata panta) in Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15, and 'confess' (homologeo) plus 'in flesh having come' (en sarki eleluthota) in 1 John 4:2. The likeness words 'likeness' (homoioma) and 'form' (schema) are the only lexical seam a contrary reading can use, and the surrounding becoming and death verbs close it.

stem_audit.notes: The question states a positive predication plus a constitutive list, body and rational soul. The body component is directly carried by the words 'flesh' (sarx), 'blood' (haima), and 'death' (thanatos) across the anchors and the Pauline parallels. The rational soul component is not carried by a dedicated 'soul' (psyche) or 'mind' (nous) anchor word in the bundle, so it is established indirectly through the unrestricted 'according to all things' (kata panta) of Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15 and through 'testing' (peirazo) and 'sympathy' (sympatheo), which require human cognitive and emotional faculties. The verdict therefore holds on the universal quantifier even though no specific interior-faculty word anchors it. The question is not tradition-loaded, so neutralized_form is null.

lay_summary: The proposition is that Jesus has a complete human nature. The Greek vocabulary across John, Hebrews, Romans, Philippians, and Galatians points the same direction, and a direct search of the text confirms the words really cluster this way rather than appearing once. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh, using 'become' (ginomai), a verb of coming to be in a state, not a verb of seeming. Hebrews 2:14 stacks two sharing verbs, 'shared in' (koinoneo) and 'partook of' (metecho), both saying Jesus partook of the same flesh and blood as the children he came to rescue, and the next verses tie this to his real death. Hebrews 2:16 contrasts taking hold of angelic nature with taking hold of 'the seed of Abraham' (sperma Abraam), that is human descent. Hebrews 2:17 and 4:15 twice use the phrase 'according to all things' (kata panta), meaning in every respect, made like the brothers and tested under the likeness of human experience, with sin alone excluded. 1 John 4:2 makes confession of Jesus come in flesh a test of true prophecy, and 4:3 brands its denial as the spirit of 'antichrist' (antichristos). The same becoming verb recurs in Romans 1:3, born of David's seed according to flesh, and Galatians 4:4, born of a woman, so the pattern is broad. Where does room for disagreement come from. It comes from one family of words. Romans 8:3 and Philippians 2:7 say he came in the 'likeness' (homoioma) of flesh and in the 'fashion' (schema) of a man, and the word for likeness can by itself mean a mere semblance. A reader could press that toward seeming rather than being. But the search shows that word is rare, and in context it is paired with the becoming verb and qualified by the word sinful, so it marks the absence of sin, not the absence of real flesh. The body is named directly, and the interior human life is required by genuine temptation and priestly sympathy, so no part of human nature is held back except sin.
